text.label: Demo report: "Loopwell" is a fictional referral platform, all data is made up
text.headline: The bottleneck: only [[9%]] of buyers ever see the invite
text.lead: While almost nobody sees the invite, polishing the share page will change very little. Fix visibility first, then the speed of the loop. In parallel, new clients need a faster launch: without it the product will not move from Revenue to Scale.
text.funnelNote: Each step's conversion relative to the previous one, last 30 days, all clients together. The constraint (TOC) is in red.
text.lensesH: The weakest lenses are PLG, the business model and the constraint itself
text.lensesP: A 0–100 score shows how much of each lens's potential the product already uses. A low score means untapped potential, not failure.
text.journeyH: The journey breaks between teams, not in the interface
text.journeyP: A simplified service blueprint from the sale to the next invite. Most of the pain sits at launch and where the buyer should see the invite.
text.matrixH: {qw} quick wins with high impact and low effort
text.matrixP: Each dot is an opportunity from the table below. Black: optimizing what exists; red outline: exploration bets.
text.opsP: ICE = impact × confidence × ease (each 1–10). The top three are highlighted. "Observed" means the finding is visible in the data or the product; "hypothesis" means it still needs testing.
text.nextH: Three steps for the next 30 days
text.nextP: Each step has a hypothesis, a success metric and the cheapest way to test it.
text.planH: Full plan: all {n} steps, most valuable first
text.planP: For each step: why it is here, what to do, the metric, effort and risk. The top three also show the alternatives considered, an experiment with a success threshold, and a pre-mortem. The top three are expanded.
text.dataH: Medium confidence: two key sources are missing
text.dataP: The report relies on a walk through the product, funnel analytics and support tickets. Competitor traffic and search demand were not checked, so the Blue Ocean and PLG scores are the least reliable.
how: Checked the connected sources and asked 4 start questions, each one skippable (one was skipped, see the answers).
Found the product stage with Lean Analytics and weighted the lenses: at Revenue, client retention and launch speed matter most.
Applied each of the 13 lenses to the journey steps. Every finding is labelled observed or hypothesis.
Scored the findings with ICE and put the system constraint (TOC) first. For the top 3, compared alternatives, wrote an experiment and ran a pre-mortem.

stage.note: Paying clients exist, so the product is at Revenue. Moving to Scale is blocked by manual launches: 31 days and 3 handoffs between teams for every new client.

route.p: 40% of those who open it share
Paid out in 5 min, no failures
The invite is never shown again

ops.t: Show the invite on the thank-you page and in the order confirmation email
Email with a personal link 7 days after delivery
"Invite shown" event on every integration + automatic tracking check after each client deploy
LTV/CAC report on referred customers for the brand's CFO
Sandbox with demo data for prospects
Managed program: the brand sets the goal, we optimize
2 interviews a week with lost deals
DTC subscription segment: reward = a free month
One owner for the whole launch journey

1.h: If we show the invite right after purchase, visibility will grow from 9% to 25% or more, because this is the moment of highest satisfaction.
1.m: Share of buyers who saw the invite
1.t: A/B test on 50% of traffic of two clients, 2 weeks

2.h: If we remind buyers of their link after delivery, the share rate will grow, because by then they have tried the product.
2.t: Manual send for one client with a control group

8.h: If we regularly hear why deals are lost, we will find 1–2 recurring barriers before building anything.
8.m: Number of interviews and patterns found
8.t: 8 calls in a month, a 5-question script

1.why: Funnel: of 120,000 purchases only 10,800 (9%) saw the invite. After that conversion is healthy: 36% open the share screen and 40% of them share. So the constraint is right here.
steps: Add the invite block to the thank-you page for every client whose integration allows it.
Add the personal link to the order confirmation email.
Turn on an A/B test: half of buyers see the new placements, half see the current flow.
After 2 weeks compare the share who saw the invite and shares per 1,000 purchases.
1.metric: Share of buyers who saw the invite (now 9%)
1.risk: Pushiness: show it once per purchase and never cover the order confirmation.
alt: Pop-up on the product page: rejected, it interrupts the purchase and risks the client's CRO.
Banner in the account area: kept as the next test, fewer people go there.
1.thr: Visibility ≥ 20% and shares per 1,000 purchases not below control
1.pm: It failed because half of the clients have a custom thank-you page and the block did not render. So check integration compatibility first (step 4).
copy: "Give a friend 15% off and get $15 after their purchase": the benefit for both in one line.
"Enjoyed it? Share with a friend and get a bonus": softer, leans on the satisfaction just felt.

2.why: New advocates are rare: 85 of 610 friends who bought (14%). There is no second invite after delivery, yet that is when satisfaction peaks. The effect is untested, so this is a hypothesis.
steps: Pick one client with enough order volume.
Set up an email 7 days after delivery with the personal link.
Split buyers into test and control groups.
Compare shares per 1,000 purchases over 30 days.
2.risk: Spam complaints: one email, easy unsubscribe, no follow-up reminders.
alt: Push notification: rejected, few clients have an app.
SMS: rejected, expensive and needs separate consent.
2.thr: +20% shares per 1,000 purchases vs control with complaints < 0.1%
2.pm: It failed because the email landed in Promotions. Test the subject and sender on a seed inbox before launch.

3.why: Launch takes 31 days on average, though sales promise 2 weeks. Most campaigns are assembled by hand from the same blocks.
steps: Take the 3 most common campaign setups.
Turn them into templates with default settings.
Measure days from signed contract to launch for every new client.
3.metric: Days from signed contract to launch (now 31)
3.risk: Templates that do not fit: let every block be changed.

4.why: Only some integrations send the invite-shown event, so 9% may be an underestimate. This is a measurement gap: without it step 1 cannot be judged fairly.
steps: List the integrations where the event is missing.
Add the event to the SDK and the docs.
After every client deploy, check automatically that events arrive.
Alert the CSM if no events arrive for more than 24 hours.
4.metric: Share of integrations sending the show event (target 100%)
4.risk: False alarms: alert only after 24 hours of silence.

5.why: The brand hires the referral program for profitable customers without extra work (JTBD), yet the report shows only shares and clicks. That the CFO needs exactly this number is still a hypothesis.
steps: Compare LTV and CAC of referred and other customers on data from 2–3 brands.
Build a one-page report for the CFO.
Show it in 3 contract renewals and collect the reaction.
5.metric: Share of renewals where the report was used in the conversation
5.risk: Incrementality: some friends would have bought anyway, so the report needs an honest estimate.

6.why: Today a brand sees value only after the sale and launch. A sandbox with demo data could shorten the sales cycle, but demand for it is untested.
steps: Run a fake door: a "Try the sandbox" button on the website.
Count clicks for 2 weeks.
If there are enough clicks, build a minimal version on demo data.
6.metric: Fake-door clicks and requests from it
6.effort: 1 day for the test, 3–4 weeks for a version
6.risk: A fake door disappoints: show an honest message and offer a demo with a person.

7.why: Some brands want an outcome, not a tool. A managed program paid for results changes the model, but needs different economics.
steps: Offer 2 clients a pilot: they set the goal and limits, we set up and optimize.
Track team hours on each pilot.
After 3 months compare the margin with the subscription.
7.metric: Pilot margin and the client's result
7.risk: Manual work eats the margin. Cap the hours.

8.why: Reasons for lost deals are recorded as one phrase in the CRM. Without regular conversations it is unclear what blocks the sale: price, integration or trust.
steps: Each week take 2 lost or stalled deals from the CRM.
A 20-minute call with a 5-question script about past decisions, not hypothetical ones.
Record quotes and tags in one table.
Once a month summarize patterns and move them to the backlog.
8.metric: 2 interviews a week and at least 1 new pattern a month
8.risk: Selling instead of researching: ask about past actions, offer nothing.
alt: A survey for lost deals: as a supplement, answers are few and shallow.
Analysing sales call recordings: kept, cheap but no substitute for conversations.
8.thr: At least 8 interviews a month and 1 backlog decision based on them
8.pm: It failed because nobody accepted the invitation. Invite from the founder's name and offer a gift for their time.

9.why: In one client's widget the "offer expires" timer resets on every page reload. This is fake urgency.
steps: Remove the timer or tie it to the real end date of the promotion.
Add a rule to the guidelines: real deadlines only.
9.metric: Complaints and unsubscribes; conversion not below control
9.risk: A small conversion drop is possible, and worth the trust it keeps.

10.why: Agencies run several brands, but each brand is set up separately. How many agencies would pay for a shared workspace is unknown.
steps: Talk to 5 partner agencies.
Describe a minimal workspace: brand list, shared templates, reports.
Decide after the interviews.
10.metric: Number of agencies ready for a pilot
10.risk: Losing focus before the constraint is solved.

11.why: DTC subscription brands are underserved by competitors, and a free month is a natural reward for a subscription. Demand is a hypothesis.
steps: Find 10 DTC brands with subscriptions.
Offer a pilot with a free-month reward.
Compare virality with current clients.
11.metric: Pilots and the share rate in pilot brands
11.risk: Being different does not mean being wanted. Build nothing before it is confirmed.

12.why: There are 3 handoffs between sales, integration and launch, and nobody owns the whole journey. Hence 31 days instead of the promised 14.
steps: Assign a launch owner for every new client.
Draw a service blueprint of the current journey and mark the waits.
Each week review clients stuck for more than 7 days.
12.metric: Days to launch and number of handoffs
12.risk: An owner without authority: give them the right to speed up other teams' work.

answers.a: More referral purchases at existing clients
Funnel analytics, support tickets, lost-deal reasons
Skipped. Assumption: no invite-visibility tests yet

Lean Analytics.d: A model where a product moves through stages: empathy, stickiness, virality, revenue, scale. Each stage has its own metrics and lenses.

Service design.d: Whether the client's whole experience works together, from the sale to launch, support and billing, not just the interface.

service blueprint.d: A diagram of the journey: what the client does, what the team does visibly and behind the scenes, and which systems support it.

Growth loops.d: One successful action starts the next: a buyer shares, a friend buys, the friend becomes an advocate.

Blue Ocean.d: Blue Ocean strategy: compete with a different kind of value where competition is still weak.

pre-mortem.d: Imagine that 3 months later the idea failed and explain why. The reasons become risks you can close in advance.

Discovery.d: Regular customer conversations and testing assumptions before building anything.

fake door.d: A button or page for a feature that does not exist yet. Clicks show demand; people are told honestly that it is coming.

thank-you.d: The page a buyer sees right after placing an order. The moment of highest satisfaction.

Sandbox.d: A safe copy of the product where everything can be tried without integration or risk.

Kaizen.d: Improving a process a little at a time: faster, fewer errors, less manual work.

JTBD.g: the job the customer hires for
JTBD.d: Jobs to Be Done: a product is hired to make progress on a job. The brand wants profitable customers without extra work, not a platform.

TOC.d: A system runs at the speed of its narrowest step. Here it is invite visibility: 9%.

CRO.d: Getting more people to the valuable action.

PLG.d: The product itself acquires customers (trial, sandbox), not only sales.

ICE.d: Impact × Confidence × Ease, each from 1 to 10. The higher the product, the sooner to start.

LTV.d: How much money a customer brings over the whole relationship.

CAC.d: How much it costs to win one new customer.

CFO.d: The person who decides whether the program pays off.

CSM.d: Looks after a client after the sale, from launch to renewal.

DTC.d: Brands that sell directly to buyers, without marketplaces or distributors.

CRM.d: The system where sales track deals, contacts and the reasons they win or lose.

SDK.d: Code the client installs on their site so the widget and events work.

A/B.d: Half of people see the new version, half the old one; the difference shows the effect.
